opus-5.5.text:
What excites me is that design is really where the value is. Simulation by itself is a means to an end. Nobody runs a fluid dynamics simulation just to watch the flow. They want a better wing, a quieter drone, a more efficient battery, a drug molecule that binds the right way. That's fundamentally an inverse problem: here's the behavior I want, now find me the shape, the material, or the parameters that produce it.

Traditionally that's been extremely painful. Numerical solvers are slow, so each forward evaluation can take hours or days on a supercomputer. Optimization needs many of those evaluations, so engineers end up exploring only a tiny corner of the design space, guided by intuition and a lot of trial and error. And the classical solvers usually aren't differentiable in a convenient way, so you can't easily get gradients to tell you which direction to move.

This is where neural operators and physics foundation models change the picture. Once you've learned the solution operator, the mapping from inputs like geometry, boundary conditions, and material properties to the full physical field, a forward evaluation becomes orders of magnitude faster. And because it's a neural network, it's differentiable end to end. So you can backpropagate through the physics to the design variables and do gradient-based optimization over very rich design spaces. You can also pair it with generative models to propose candidate designs, then evaluate and refine them in the loop.

Operators are a natural fit because they work in function space. They aren't tied to one mesh or resolution, so you can train on data from many sources at different fidelities, explore designs cheaply at coarse resolution, and then zoom in. That's essential for real engineering, where geometries vary wildly.

The foundation model angle matters because data in science is expensive and fragmented. If you pretrain across many kinds of PDEs and physical systems, you get something that transfers. A new design problem then needs much less task-specific data, much like fine-tuning in language.

The other piece I care about is trust. In inverse design, the optimizer will happily exploit any error in your surrogate and find a "design" that only works in the model's imagination. So you have to bake in physics: physics-informed losses, constraints, checking candidates against high-fidelity solvers, and uncertainty estimates so you know when you're extrapolating. When you get that right, you go from AI as a fast approximator to AI as a genuine design partner, one that proposes things humans might never have thought of, and that can actually be built and tested. We've seen that in examples like designing medical catheters to reduce bacterial contamination, where the AI-proposed geometry was manufactured and validated in the lab. That closed loop from model to real physical artifact is what really gets me excited.

r001.rationale: It explains that a learned solution operator makes forward evaluations fast and differentiable, allowing optimization through the physics to find design variables.

r002.rationale: It describes baking physics into the process through constraints and checking proposed candidates against high-fidelity solvers to prevent designs that only work in the surrogate.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So, what really excites me here is that for most of the history of science and engineering, we've been stuck in the forward direction. You have a design, you simulate it, you see how it performs. If you want a better design, you tweak something and simulate again. And when each simulation takes hours or days on a supercomputer, you can only afford to try a handful of candidates. So you end up with designs that are good enough, not designs that are optimal.

What I actually care about is the inverse question. Don't tell me how this wing performs. Tell me what wing I should build to get the lift and drag I want. Tell me what catheter geometry minimizes bacterial contamination. Tell me what material composition gives me this band gap. That's the question engineers and scientists actually have, and classical numerical solvers are terrible at answering it, because they are not differentiable in any practical sense and they are far too slow to sit inside an optimization loop.

This is where neural operators change the picture completely. Once you have a model that has learned the solution operator of the underlying PDEs, so it maps from the design, the geometry, the boundary conditions, directly to the physical fields, two things happen. First, inference is orders of magnitude faster than the solver, often thousands of times faster, so you can explore a vast design space instead of a dozen points. Second, and this is the part people underappreciate, the model is differentiable end to end. You can take gradients of your objective with respect to the design itself and just walk downhill. You turn design into an optimization problem that gradient descent can actually solve.

And when we did this, for example with the catheter work, the designs we got back were not things a human would have sketched. The optimizer found geometries that reduced bacterial upstream swimming by a huge factor, and then we 3D-printed them and validated them experimentally. That loop, from learned physics to novel design to physical validation, is what I find so compelling. It's a different way of doing engineering.

The foundation model aspect matters because you don't want to train from scratch for every new domain. If a model has absorbed a broad range of physics, fluids, structures, electromagnetics, different geometries and resolutions, then it can be adapted quickly to a new design problem with limited data, and it generalizes to regimes it hasn't exactly seen. There are real challenges there. You need to respect conservation laws, handle multiple scales, quantify uncertainty so the optimizer doesn't exploit regions where the model is simply wrong. But I think the trajectory is clear. We're moving from AI that predicts physics to AI that invents in physics, and the inverse problem is where that happens.

r001.rationale: The response describes a learned physics model rapidly mapping designs to physical fields, then using gradients of the objective to optimize the design.

r002.rationale: It mentions conservation laws and uncertainty to keep the optimizer from exploiting model errors, but does not clearly state that physics-accurate models serve as guardrails for AI-generated designs.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that we can move from predicting what a design will do to asking what design will give us the behavior we want. In the forward problem, you specify the geometry, the materials, and the operating conditions, and then simulate the physics. In the inverse problem, you start with an objective and search for a design that achieves it.

That search can be very expensive if every candidate requires a new simulation. A physics foundation model could make those predictions much faster, so we can explore more possibilities. And if the model is differentiable, we can use its gradients to guide how we change the design.

But the key is that the design still has to work under the actual physics. An optimizer can find weaknesses in your model just as easily as it can find a good solution. So I see this as a loop: use the model to explore and propose designs, validate them with high-fidelity simulation or experiments, and use that feedback to improve the model. That opens up a much more ambitious design space.

r001.rationale: The response describes using a physics foundation model to make predictions during design search, explore candidates, and guide design changes toward an objective.

r002.rationale: It calls for validating proposed designs against actual physics, but does not state that physics-accurate models serve as guardrails for AI-generated optimized designs.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that we can move from asking, “How will this design behave?” to asking, “What design will give us the behavior we want?” Traditionally, you propose a design, run an expensive simulation, and repeat. That makes it difficult to explore a large space of possibilities.

With a physics foundation model, the idea is to learn a reusable model of the underlying physics, so you can evaluate candidate designs much faster. And if that model is differentiable, you can use its gradients to guide the search toward your objective, subject to constraints.

But the interesting challenge is that optimization will find weaknesses in your model. So you need to account for uncertainty and validate promising designs with high-fidelity simulations or experiments. The opportunity is to make that whole discovery loop faster—and potentially find designs that we wouldn’t have thought to try.

r001.rationale: It says the physics model can quickly evaluate candidate designs and use gradients to guide the search toward the desired behavior, communicating model-based simulation within optimization.

r002.rationale: It recommends accounting for uncertainty and validating promising designs with high-fidelity simulations or experiments, but does not state that physics-accurate models serve as guardrails for AI-generated optimized designs.
